newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-MASTERS VICTORY IS DREAM COME TRUE, EVEN IF LATE.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-MASTERS VICTORY IS DREAM COME TRUE, EVEN IF LATE.

text.p: The record-setting, awe-inspiring victory by Tiger Woods in the Masters on Sunday was a dream come true for the golfing phenomenon -- although it came later than the supremely confident 21 year old had expected.

"I thought I could win (the Masters) when I was 19. That's when I first played here and I expected myself to win the tournament," Woods said after capturing a coveted Masters green jacket on his third try, but first as a professional.

Woods, who was introduced to golf by his father before he could walk, said he had always fantasized about winning the Masters, although even he did not dream his first victory would be so spectacular -- with a record score of 270 and a record winning margin of 12 strokes.
"It's not what you envision," said Woods, who began winning national golf championships as a young teenager -- after demonstrating his golf swing on television at age 5.

Like many youngsters, Woods envisioned himself battling on the back nine of Augusta National against the likes of Jack Nicklaus, Tom Watson or Nick Faldo -- not trouncing the best golfers in the world like he did on Sunday.
"That's just something that you never really dream of," Woods said just after Faldo helped him don the first of what everyone -- including Woods -- expects to be many green jackets.
Asked how the jacket -- actually a borrowed one -- fit, Woods said "perfect."
The young Californian had been groomed for golfing greatness almost from birth by his father, Earl, a former U.S. Army "green beret" officer who took up the game when he was in his 40s.
When Tiger was just 6 months old, he sat in a high-chair and watched his father practice his golf swing. By the time he was 8 years old he was winning international tournaments.
He has been winning tournaments ever since -- including a record three consecutive U.S. Junior championships and an unprecedented three U.S. Amateur championships in a row.
Woods then turned pro and won three of the first nine tournaments he entered -- setting the stage for his first victory in a major championship.
"I told him dreams can be turned into reality," the elder Woods said after his son did just that -- fulfilling one of his and his father's most cherished dreams.

"It's a wonderful thing to see someone live up to his dreams," added the proud father, who admitted that there was a time when he feared he might not live to see his son win the Masters. Woods, 64, underwent heart bypass surgery six weeks ago and admitted that the doctors "almost didn't save me."
Woods said that his son has been so successful in golf not just because of his prodigious physical talents, which include hitting the ball farther than anyone in the game.
"He has a creative mind that is so resourceful that he sees escape routes that aren't obvious to other players," father said of son.
"That's why he's so dangerous. It's play for him, not work. He loves it.
"He has been talking about winning the Masters since he was 5 years old. I just told him he'd have to grow up."
Perhaps because the newest -- and youngest -- Masters champion started the game at such an early age he sees an important impact of his victory as the influence it will have on young people.

"I think (my) winning here is going to do a lot for the game of golf," Woods said. "A lot of kids will start playing it now. I think that now kids will think golf is cool and they'll start playing it."
Meanwhile, Woods had his own ambitions -- for both the near and distant future.
Asked what his immediate plans were, the practical Tiger Woods said: "Eat, celebrate, pack and move on."
Asked about the more distant future, the ultra-confident and unabashed Tiger Woods said: "I know my goal is to be the best. I expect nothing but the best for myself."
